title: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Outline of the Principle” (from p. 716), pp. 716–717. Scope: essentially all processes in nature, mathematics and engineered systems whose behavior is not obviously simple

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.27

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Finite formal families permit partial empirical and mathematical tests. Existing resources cannot resolve 'almost all' across nature, mathematics, and engineered systems or establish a unique maximal sophistication notion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define obvious simplicity, a sampling distribution over a bounded formal system family, and sophistication as computational universality, then estimate the universal fraction using proofs and certified simulations. Repeating this across families tests restricted versions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Universality is undecidable in general.

There is no canonical measure over all processes.

Natural processes cannot be exhaustively sampled or assigned exact rules.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Restricted to a small formal family, the principle becomes a statement about what fraction of non-simple rules are universal, and a few rules on each side are already classified. The stated scope is almost all processes in nature, mathematics, and engineering, for which no such classification exists. Intermediate degrees are a published rival formalization, so even the mathematical reading is not unique.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Operationalize obviously simple as proved repetitive or nested behavior, and equivalent sophistication as Turing universality. Inside a finite rule family, estimate the fraction of non-simple rules that are universal. The principle is supported if that fraction is near one across families and if sampled natural processes match it, and it is refuted by a large class of non-simple, non-universal processes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A system can look complex for decades without a universality proof, and that delay is compatible with the principle.

Almost all, obviously simple, and sophistication admit several formalizations, including intermediate degrees and complexity classes.
